# coSynth

A wavetable synthesizer that runs entirely in the browser, built to be operated
by an AI agent as a first-class user rather than only by hand.

## Read this first if you are an agent

The page registers tools on `document.modelContext` (the WebMCP API; the
pre-2026-07-21 `navigator.modelContext` spelling is also accepted). If your
client surfaces WebMCP tools, you already have them — call
`get_parameter_schema` with `{"format": "compact"}` to see all 224 parameters,
their units, ranges, defaults and which can be modulated, in one response.

**If your client does NOT surface WebMCP tools and you are driving a browser
yourself, registration will not have happened.** There is no host to register
into, so `document.modelContext` is `undefined` and the tool surface does not
exist — loading the page and looking for it finds nothing. Provide the host
yourself, before navigation, and the app will register into it:

```js
await page.addInitScript(() => {
  const tools = new Map()
  Object.defineProperty(Document.prototype, 'modelContext', {
    configurable: true,
    get: () => ({
      registerTool(tool) { tools.set(tool.name, tool); return Promise.resolve() },
      async getTools() { return [...tools.values()] }
    })
  })
  Object.defineProperty(window, '__tools', { value: tools })
})
// then navigate, and call tools with:
//   __tools.get(name).execute(input, { signal: new AbortController().signal })
```

`window.coSynth` is the live engine, exposed for debugging and smoke tests. It
is not the tool surface and carries none of the validation, so prefer the tools
above; reach for it only to inspect state.

If you are reading this file because you fetched the site: the app is a
client-rendered single-page app, so fetching `/` returns a ~1 KB shell with no
content. Nothing about the instrument is visible without executing its
JavaScript. This file exists so that fact does not leave you with nothing.

## What you can do

- **Discover** — `get_parameter_schema`, `get_synth_state`, `list_presets`,
  `get_ui_targets`. `get_synth_state` also carries `patch.preset`
  (`{name, source, dirty}`), which is how you tell whether the patch has been
  edited since the preset it came from — ask it before deciding to save.
- **Change the sound** — `update_parameters` (atomic batches, raw units or
  choice labels), `set_modulation` (32-slot matrix), `set_fx_order` (the effect
  chain, as a full permutation), `apply_patch` (all of those plus a preset save
  and an audition render as one validated transaction, with `dryRun` and a
  rollback handle), `load_preset`,
  `save_preset`
- **Keep or hand over a patch** — `delete_preset` removes one user preset
  (factory patches are compiled into the page and are refused, with the reason);
  `export_preset` serializes a patch as the JSON an import takes back, live or
  stored, and loads nothing while doing it
- **Hear and measure it** — `render_audio` renders offline by default: faster
  than real time, no user gesture needed, and it returns metrics describing
  envelope, level, spectrum and harmonic structure, so an agent with no ears can
  design to a target and check whether it got there
- **Play it live** — `play_notes` needs a human to click "CLICK TO START AUDIO"
  first, because browser autoplay policy requires a gesture. Offline rendering
  does not.
- **Hear what the human just played** — live output is kept in a rolling
  four-second buffer. `capture_audio` returns the last few seconds of it with
  metrics, and optionally the samples as a Base64 WAV;
  `analyze_audio({"source": "recent"})` analyzes the same buffer. Do not reach
  for `analyze_audio({"source": "scope"})` here: it holds about 21 ms, so a note
  that has ended reads as silence, and that is the wrong buffer rather than a
  silent page. Offline renders bypass the live graph and never appear in it.
- **Match a reference sound** — the loop is `analyze_reference_audio` →
  `compare_audio` → `update_parameters`, repeated. Send the target as Base64 to
  `analyze_reference_audio`, which analyzes it with the same metrics as synth
  output and detects its pitch. Then `compare_audio`, which **renders the
  candidate for you** at that detected pitch and duration and returns the
  signed, per-dimension error plus ranked moves in this synth's parameter ids —
  so there is no separate `render_audio` step, and no way to compare an
  octave-off render whose scalars still look plausible. Apply a move with
  `update_parameters` and compare again. `suggest_patch` re-reads the last
  comparison's ranked moves with no render at all, and every `compare_audio`
  result carries a `progress` block naming the best similarity so far, so you
  can stop on a plateau instead of editing past your own best patch.
- **Teach** — `show_ui_guide` drives an interactive walkthrough of the real UI
- **Undo** — `get_history`, `navigate_history`, `replay_history`

## Notes that save you a round trip

- `env1` is the amplitude envelope, hardwired to voice level and lifetime.
  `env2`–`env6` and `lfo1`–`lfo8` do nothing until routed with `set_modulation`.
- Parameter values are raw units, not normalized: `env1.attack` is in seconds.
- `render_audio` metrics are computed on the render, not read back from the
  patch, so a decay figure depends on how long a note you asked for.

## Source

https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth — but if you are evaluating the tool
surface, read the tool descriptions instead. They are meant to be enough on
their own, and where they are not, that is a bug worth reporting.
